Some information about Intel processors (recalling from memory).

Back in the old days, the processor had access to every single part of memory and IO ports. And every single program could get hold directly to the hard disks and memory. This is very annoying because when a program had a bug it brought down the complete OS. A reboots was required.

So Intel created rings 0 to 3 where any software running at ring 0 had IO access, more instructions and more memory access, while and any software running at higher levels did not have this much access.

How the rings are used depends on the OS. For a very long time Windows up to NT 3.5 still allowed (video driver) programs to have direct access to ring 0 because jumping from ring 3 to 0 hits a performance penalty. And back in those days computers were still slow.

It all changed with Windows NT 4 where software did have to go through a driver that then passed the information to ring 0. Since then, Windows became more stable because programs did not have direct control over the video card anymore. But drivers were needed to be rewritten. A lot of hardware did not work on the newer NT 4.0.

Actually it was NT 3.5 and earlier that ran the graphics driver completely in user space. Full user space graphics driver performance kinda sucked though so in NT 4.0 they moved the graphics driver back to the executive layer which was ring 0 (subsequently this was the first version of NT that supported DirectX). So yes, drivers needed to be rewritten for NT 4.0 but this was to support kernel mode operation (and bad drivers could take down the system).

This kernel level driver model was carried through into win2k and XP as the windows 2000 Display Driver Model (XDDM).

With Vista, Microsoft introduced the Windows Display Driver Model which split the graphics driver between the kernel and user space. This hybrid model tries to minimize the amount of kernel space driver to the core performance critical parts. It provides improved fault-tolerance but does require certain hardware features (like shader 2.0).

Vista and Win7 supported both models (XDDM and WDDM). Windows 8 and newer only support versions of WDDM.

Syscalls and drivers are the two main ways for a user to get to ring 0. By exploiting a vulnerable driver or syscall a malicious user could inject code into ring 0. Alternatively a malicious user could trick somebody into installing a driver that contains the code. Or a rootkit that modifies the kernal itself could do it.

Ring -1 was introduced to support hypervisors (virtual machine monitors) which then run multiple virtual machines that each run their own OS.

Ring -2, or more correctly, System Management Mode is not intended to be accessed by normal programs (including the OS). It runs special software, typically provided by firmware, that executes below the OS. It is mainly used to handle hardware interations like handling memory/chipset errors, hardware emulation, power/thermal management, security (Trusted Platform Module) etc...

The SMM is entered via the System Management Interrupt (SMI) which the OS cannot override or disable so once you get code into the SMM the OS is essentially powerless from preventing it to run (eventually).

It should be noted, in theory, code runing in ring 0 can't access or modify the code run by SMM which is typically loaded by hardware at boot. This hack apparenlty exploits certain hardware features to load code into the SMM which otherwise wouldn't be possible.

The design flaw here is, a certain sequence of assembler instructions could make the CPU confused and think that you are running at level 0. The payload can then modify your boot sector.

Actually, the vulnerability dicussed here requires that you already run code in ring 0. Modern processors also have a ring -1 and -2. Ring -1 is for virtualisation, allowing you to run a hypervisor in ring -1 and run any number of guest operating systems, giving each full access to rings 0-3. Ring -2 is System Management Mode, for BIOS code, advanced power control, hardware debugging, TPM emulation and the like.

The design flaw here now allows you to jump from ring 0 to ring -2, bypassing hypervisors and giving you more hardware access. Being in ring -2 also allows you to hide memory you use from the operating system, allowing really sneaky rootkits.

All modern operating systems expect that their kernel and driver code is running in [Ring 0] privileged mode, which of course is fine in a non-virtualized PC. However, in a virtual machine, you don't want that kernel and driver code, or the interrupt handlers, to really have full control over the hardware; you need the VMM to be able to be able to transparently manage the system. But because both the VMM itself, and the virtualized guest operating system kernel and drivers are running in Ring 0 -- in other words, they're peers -- the VMM has to do a lot of work to maintain control of the guest operating system. Thus, the emulation, and the performance hit that it represents.

So in the old days you had ring 0 where you had direct hardware controller access.

Because Virtualization came out, and and software is not designed for ring 0 to cooperate with other OS, they moved the real hardware controller access one layer deeper in the Intel chip. Old OS still worked, and newer VM software can control the real hardware controller access.
